p6-146.text: An investigation of the rate of cooling of a thermometer bulb positioned directly above a constant-temperature hot water bath (position A) compared to positioned in room air away from the bath (position B). Part (a) asks to read the water bath temperature from a thermometer diagram. Part (b) involves completing table units, identifying which position cools faster in the first 30 seconds with justification, calculating overall temperature changes between 30 s and 180 s, and estimating room temperature. Part (c) requires a practical precaution for reliable readings, and part (d) asks for two conditions to keep constant when repeating the experiment.

p6-147.text: Students investigate four methods of cooling hot water: stirring (Experiment A), pouring between beakers (Experiment B), cooling with a lid (Experiment C), and cooling without a lid (Experiment D). The student reads initial and final temperatures from three thermometer diagrams, calculates the temperature drops, and ranks all four cooling methods in order of greatest temperature drop. Finally, the student identifies two control variables required for reliable results when repeating the experiment and suggests how to make the comparison fairer.

p6-148.text: Students investigate methods of reducing thermal energy loss using beaker A (insulated, open top) and beaker B (uninsulated, with a lid). The student reads initial temperatures from thermometer diagrams, completes table headings with units, and inserts time values. The student determines which beaker loses thermal energy faster, justifying the answer using the data, states a control variable for a fair test, and suggests a modification to the experimental setup to evaluate insulation effectiveness independently.

p6-149.text: An investigation into the heating of a thermometer bulb placed at different distances from a lamp. In part (a), candidates read room temperature from a thermometer scale. In part (b), they complete distance values and column headings in a data table. In part (c), they calculate the difference between the temperature reading above the lamp and the reading at the same horizontal distance beside it. In part (d), candidates suggest two control variables needed to investigate heat transfer by radiation and convection. In part (e), they state a practical precaution to obtain reliable results.

p6-150.text: An investigation into the rate of cooling of hot water in a beaker. In part (a), candidates read room temperature from a thermometer diagram. In part (b), they plot a graph of temperature against time using given data from a table. In part (c), candidates suggest two differences in environmental conditions across different laboratories, such as room temperature or air draughts, that could affect the rate of cooling and produce different graphs.

p6-151.text: An investigation of the rate of cooling of hot water in a beaker over a 150-second period. In part (a), candidates read the room temperature from a thermometer diagram. In part (b), candidates plot a graph of water temperature against time using given table readings. In part (c), candidates suggest two environmental conditions in different laboratories, such as ambient room temperature or air draughts, that could affect the cooling rate and lead to different graph curves.

p6-152.text: An investigation compares the cooling rate of two different volumes of hot water, 150 cm^3 and 250 cm^3, over 150 seconds. In part (a), candidates record the room temperature shown on a thermometer diagram. In part (b), candidates complete the table column headers with appropriate units and draw a conclusion comparing the cooling rates of the two volumes based on table data. In part (c), candidates suggest two control variables needed to ensure reliable results when repeating the experiment.

p6-153.text: An investigation into the cooling rate of hot water. Students read room temperature from a thermometer diagram and calculate initial temperature differences above room temperature as well as total temperature drop after 100 seconds for hot water. The experiment is repeated with warm water formed by mixing hot and cold water. Students determine whether the rate of temperature change is proportional to the difference between starting temperature and room temperature by evaluating given ratios. Finally, they identify two variables that must be controlled when repeating the experiment to check results.

p6-154.text: An experiment comparing how white and black surfaces absorb thermal radiation from a lamp. Students take an initial temperature reading from a thermometer diagram and complete column headings with appropriate units in a table. They calculate overall temperature changes for white and black cards over 300 seconds and identify which surface absorbs thermal radiation more efficiently. They also evaluate whether the rate of temperature rise is higher at the start than at the end of the experiment using black card data, and suggest a precaution needed to ensure a fair test.

p6-156.text: A student investigates the position of the image formed in a plane mirror using a ray-trace sheet. The student marks pin positions for incident and reflected rays at angles of incidence 30° and 40°. The question asks to place a pin position P2, draw and extend reflected rays to find their intersection point Y, and measure perpendicular distances from object pin P1 and intersection point Y to the mirror line MR. The student also locates image pin P8 along the normal line, measures distance x, completes a diagram showing the appearance of pins over/in the mirror, draws conclusions comparing image and object distances, and identifies practical sources of inaccuracy.

p6-157.text: A student determines the focal length of a converging lens using two different methods with an illuminated triangle object, lens, and screen. In Method 1, the student measures diagram distances u and v, calculates actual distances U and V using a scale factor, and calculates the focal length f1. In Method 2, the lens is moved closer to the screen to form another image; the student measures image distance v, height of object h_O, and height of image h_I, calculates magnification M, and determines a second focal length f2. The question also assesses experimental techniques for obtaining sharp images, precautions for accurate measurement, and evaluation of method accuracy.

p6-158.text: A student investigates the reflection of light using a plane mirror on a ray-trace sheet. The task involves measuring an angle θ, drawing a normal to line AB at point N and extending it to line CD at point L, evaluating if a ray-tracing point P is positioned at a suitable distance from N, drawing line NP to intersect line CD at point G, and measuring length LG. Using a given set of results in a table, students plot a graph of distance a against angle θ. Finally, students identify a potential source of inaccuracy and suggest an improvement to check the reliability of the results.

p6-159.text: Students plan an investigation to determine the relationship between the thickness t of a converging lens and its focal length f. Available apparatus includes an illuminated object, lenses of different thicknesses in a holder, a screen, a metre rule, a 30 cm ruler, and two rectangular wooden blocks. The plan requires drawing a labelled diagram of the setup showing object distance u and image distance v, describing the experimental method and measurements, explaining how to determine lens thickness t using wooden blocks and ruler, and designing a suitable table for displaying the data.

p6-160.text: A student determines the focal length f of a lens using an illuminated object, lens, and screen setup. The distance d on a scale diagram is measured and converted to actual distance D. Using object distance u and image distance v, focal lengths are calculated using f = uv/D and recorded in a table. An average focal length f_A is calculated to a suitable number of significant figures. The student states a precaution for accurate readings. The screen position is then altered to calculate a new distance D and focal length f, which is compared with f_A to assess agreement within experimental accuracy.

p6-161.text: Students determine the focal length of a converging lens using two methods. In Method 1, object distance u and image distance v are measured from a scale diagram, scaled to actual values U and V, and used to calculate focal length f_1 using f_1 = UV/(U + V). A technique for obtaining a sharp image is described. In Method 2, object and image heights are measured to calculate magnification M and determine focal length f_2 using f_2 = V/(M + 1). The two focal length values are compared, a precaution for reliability is given, and the relative accuracy of the two methods is evaluated.

p6-162.text: An optics experiment is performed to determine the focal length f of a lens using an illuminated object, a converging lens, and a screen. The distance D between the object and screen is set to various values, and the object distance u and image distance v are recorded. Part (a) asks to calculate and record values of uv in a table. Part (b) requires plotting a graph of uv against D. Part (c) asks to determine the gradient G of the line. Part (d) requires stating the focal length f to a suitable number of significant figures. Part (e) asks for two experimental difficulties in obtaining accurate readings.

p6-163.text: An experiment is conducted to determine the focal length of a thin converging lens using an illuminated object and a screen. Part (a) asks to measure the image distance v from a scaled diagram, calculate the actual image distance V using the scale factor, and calculate the focal length f_1 using a given lens formula. Part (b) asks to calculate an average focal length f_A from f_1 and a provided second measurement f_2, rounded to a suitable number of significant figures. Part (c) asks to suggest additional object distances U to improve reliability. Part (d) requires stating two practical precautions for obtaining accurate readings.

p6-164.text: A student investigates the image produced by a converging lens using an illuminated triangular-shaped object and a screen. First, she measures the height h_o of the object from a full-size diagram. Next, she records the image height h_I for various object distances u and calculates N = h_o / h_I. She plots a graph of u against N, determines its gradient G, and discusses a difficulty in measuring image height along with an improvement.

p6-165.text: A student determines the refractive index n of a transparent block using a ray-tracing experiment. On a diagram showing the block's outline ABCD, the student draws a normal, a ray at an angle of incidence i = 30°, and uses optical pins P_1, P_2, P_3, and P_4 to trace the refracted ray. The student measures lengths a and b to calculate n using a given equation, repeats the procedure for i = 45°, identifies experimental difficulties causing discrepancies in n, and selects the most sensible precaution for reliable results.

p6-166.text: A student determines the refractive index of a transparent glass block using ray-tracing pins. On a provided outline of the block ABCD, the student draws a normal, an incident ray at an angle of incidence i = 30°, and places pins P1 and P2. Looking through the opposite side CD, the student aligns pins P3 and P4 to trace the emergent ray. The student measures lengths a and b to calculate the refractive index n using the formula n = a / b. Finally, the student suggests additional angles of incidence to improve reliability and states a practical precaution.

p6-167.text: A student investigates the reflection of light by a plane mirror on a ray-trace sheet. First, the student measures the angle alpha between reference line AN and mirror line CD. A normal LN is drawn at point N, and pins P1 and P2 are placed on it. A mirror is placed on CD, and pins P3 and P4 are aligned with the images. The student draws the reflected ray and measures the angle theta between the ray and the normal. The experiment is repeated with the mirror moved to line EF at an angle alpha = 35°, using pins P5 and P6. The student records angles in a table, justifies whether the change in theta equals twice the change in alpha, and states two experimental precautions.

p6-168.text: Students investigate the magnification produced by a converging lens using an illuminated triangle, lens, and screen on a bench. In part (a), the student measures the image height hI from a diagram. In part (b), magnification M is calculated for various object distances u using M = hI / ho. Part (c) requires plotting a graph of M against u. Part (d) asks to determine u when M = 1.0 from the graph. Part (e) asks for a difficulty and improvement when measuring image height, and part (f) requires explaining why ensuring components are perpendicular to the bench is an important precaution.

p6-169.text: A class investigates the refraction of light passing through a transparent glass block using optics pins and a ray-trace sheet. In part (a), a normal and an incident ray at an angle of 30 degrees are drawn, and pin positions are indicated. In part (b), emergent ray positions are joined using pins P3 and P4. Part (c) requires measuring angle alpha and length x. Part (d) compares results with another angle of incidence and justifies whether the data supports a student's suggestion. Part (e) asks for one experimental precaution for reliable ray tracing results.

p6-170.text: A student investigates the refraction of light passing through a transparent block using optics pins. On a ray-trace sheet showing a glass block ABCD, the student draws a normal NL, an incident ray FE at 40^o to the normal, and marks pin positions. By viewing through side CD, the student places pins P_3 and P_4 to trace the emerging ray. The line is extended to the normal, and angle alpha and length x are measured. The procedure is repeated for an angle of incidence on the other side of the normal, giving angle beta and length y. Students evaluate whether results support a suggestion that corresponding angles and lengths should be equal, and state an experimental precaution.

p6-171.text: A class investigates images formed on a screen using a converging lens. Given a lens with a focal length of 15.0 cm, students suggest a suitable distance D between the illuminated object and the screen. Methods to find the best focused screen position reliably are discussed. Using given object distance u = 15.0 cm and image distance v = 29.7 cm, the focal length f is calculated using the formula f = uv / (u + v) to a suitable number of significant figures with units. Differences between the object and image appearance are noted, and sensible experimental procedures among options A to F are selected.

p6-172.text: A student investigates the refraction and reflection of light using a transparent glass block, pins, a mirror, and a ray-trace sheet. Part (a) asks to measure angle theta. Part (b) suggests a suitable distance between pins. Part (c) involves drawing normals, line extensions, and measuring lengths a and b to calculate the refractive index n using n = a / b. Part (d) uses a plane mirror against the block to trace reflected rays, measure angle alpha, and compare it with theta. Part (e) asks for a source of experimental inaccuracy in ray-tracing.

p6-173.text: A student determines the focal length f of a lens using an illuminated object, a converging lens, and a screen on a bench. Part (a) measures distance v and total distance d from a scale diagram drawn to 1/10th actual size. Part (b) calculates actual distances and the product UV to fill Table 2.1. Part (c) asks to state a difference in the image when object distance U changes. Part (d) calculates focal length values f1 and f2, and finds their average. Part (e) asks for sources of difficulty in obtaining reliable results. Part (f) requires planning by suggesting a suitable number and range of values for U to draw a graph.

p6-174.text: A student determines the focal length f of a lens using an illuminated object, lens, and screen. Table 3.1 gives values of image distance v for various object distances u. (a) Students plot v against u on a grid and draw a best-fit curve. (b) They mark specific points to draw a straight line intersection, recording coordinates u_1 and v_1, and calculate focal length f using a given formula. (c) Students suggest two differences between the illuminated object and the image appearance (e.g., inverted, magnified/diminished). (d) Two precautions for obtaining reliable readings in lens experiments are requested, such as carrying out the experiment in a dark room or ensuring the lens is perpendicular to the bench.

p6-175.text: A student plans an experiment to determine the focal length f of a converging lens using the equation f = uv / (u + v). Provided apparatus includes a lens holder, a 12V lamp in a holder with power supply, and a card with a triangular hole covered with tracing paper. The student must list additional apparatus needed (such as a metre rule and a screen), draw a labelled diagram showing the arrangement with distances u and v, write a step-by-step method describing how to obtain a focused image and calculate f, state precautions for obtaining a clear focused image (such as using a darkened room), and state precautions for accurate measurements (such as viewing perpendicularly to avoid parallax).

p6-176.text: A student investigates the refraction of light using a transparent glass block ABCD and a ray-trace sheet. Part (a) asks to draw a normal to line AB at point N extending to line CD, label the crossing point L, and measure angle theta between the normal and line NM. Part (b) asks to mark appropriate positions for pins P1 and P2 on line NM. Part (c) involves joining P3 and P4, finding intersection points E and F, measuring lengths a and b, and calculating the refractive index n = a / b. Part (d) requires describing two experimental precautions.

p6-177.text: A student determines the focal length of a converging lens using an illuminated object, lens, and screen. Part (a) requires measuring distances u and v from the diagram. Part (b) involves calculating actual distances using scale and finding focal length f1 using a given formula. Part (c) asks to calculate an average focal length from a table of repeat values. Part (d) requires discussing whether experimental results confirm that u equals v when u = 2f, given measurements of x and y. Part (e) asks for two precautions to obtain reliable results in the lens investigation.

p6-178.text: A student investigates lens magnification using an illuminated object, a converging lens, and a screen fixed at a total distance D = 80.0 cm. In part (a), the student measures object distance a and image distance b for an enlarged image, and calculates the magnification m_1. In part (b), the student moves the lens to find a smaller image, measures distances x and y, and calculates m_2. In part (c), the student evaluates whether m_1 multiplied by m_2 equals 1. In parts (d) and (e), the student suggests experimental precautions and explains the difficulty in finding the sharpest focus.

p6-179.text: A student plans an experiment to investigate how the size of an image varies with object distance for a converging lens. The plan must include a labelled diagram of the apparatus, instructions for carrying out the experiment, factors limiting the range of object distances, the graph to be plotted, and one experimental precaution with an explanation of the effect of not taking it.

p6-180.text: A student investigates refraction through a transparent rectangular block. The student draws an incident line FE at an angle i = 20° to the normal on a ray trace diagram and marks a suitable pin position P, explaining why the pin position is chosen for accuracy. The student measures angle θ on the diagram and records it in a table of results for different values of i. A graph of θ against i is plotted, and the student calculates the gradient G of the graph showing working.

p6-181.text: A student investigates reflection using a plane mirror. The student measures length l of line AB on a ray-trace diagram and marks a suitable position for pin P_2. Pin positions P_3 and P_4 are placed to trace the reflected ray, defining distance d on line XY. Given a set of readings for angle of incidence i and distance d, a graph of d against i is plotted. The student evaluates whether i is directly proportional to d using the graph and suggests two practical difficulties in obtaining accurate readings.

p6-182.text: An investigation to determine the focal length of a converging lens using two different methods. Students measure the height of an illuminated triangular object and its image on a screen to calculate magnification M and focal length f_1. They identify a practical difficulty in measuring image height and propose an improvement. Next, they measure the distance between the lens and screen on a 1/5th scale diagram to determine actual image distance v and calculate a second focal length f_2. Finally, they judge whether f_1 and f_2 support the suggestion that they should be equal and state a precaution to make the experiment reliable.

p6-183.text: An optics experiment assessing the focal length of a small converging lens. A student measures full-size diagram distances u_1 (object to lens) and v_1 (lens to screen) for a sharp image and calculates the focal length f using a given formula. Keeping the object and screen fixed, the lens is shifted to find a second sharp image, and the new object distance u_2 is measured. The student determines whether u_2 and v_1 are equal, supporting their conclusion with data. Finally, the student describes two practical precautions required to obtain reliable results in lens experiments.

p6-184.text: A student investigates the refraction of light through a transparent block using a ray-trace sheet, pins, and a glass block. Students draw a normal, incident ray lines at a given angle, place pins to trace the emergent ray, measure lengths between specific intersection points on the ray trace sheet, and calculate the refractive index using a given formula. Additional parts ask for experimental precautions and drawing the correct position of a ray box as an alternative to pins.

p6-185.text: A student investigates reflection using a plane mirror, ray-trace sheet, and optical pins. The student labels the normal, positions two pins on an incident line, and views their reflections to locate the reflected ray when the mirror is tilted at various angles theta. Data for angle alpha versus angle theta is recorded in a table. The student plots a graph of alpha against theta, determines direct proportionality from the graph line, and suggests sources of experimental inaccuracy.

p6-186.text: A class investigates the image formed by a converging lens using an illuminated object, a lens, and a screen. Given measured distances u and v, part (a) asks to calculate the focal length f using a provided formula and give the answer to a suitable number of significant figures. Part (b) asks to state two precautions for obtaining reliable measurements. Part (c) asks to suggest two differences between the appearance of the illuminated triangular object and its well-focused image on the screen.

p6-187.text: A student determines the focal length of a converging lens by two methods. First, using an illuminated object, lens, and mirror, part (a) asks to measure distance f on a scaled diagram and calculate the actual focal length F, recording it in a table. Part (b) calculates an average value F1. Part (c) uses a lens, illuminated object, and screen setup to find F2 from distances u and v, then asks whether F1 and F2 are equal with justification. Part (d) requires describing a precaution to obtain reliable results.

p6-188.text: The class investigates reflection using a plane mirror on a ray-trace sheet. Students draw a normal, an incident ray at an angle of 30 degrees, and position pins to locate the reflected ray. Part (a) asks to draw a normal line NL crossing MR at point A, and an 8.0 cm incident line AB. Part (b) labels a suitable position for pin P2. Part (c) involves extending the line through P3 and P4 to meet NL and measuring angle r. Part (d) requires stating two precautions for reliable readings. Part (e) asks for a practical reason why the reflected ray might differ from theory.

p6-189.text: The class performs a lens experiment to determine the focal length using an illuminated object, a converging lens, and a screen. Part (a) requires drawing a diagram showing how the apparatus is arranged on a laboratory bench. Part (b) asks for a suitable distance d between the illuminated object and the screen given a focal length of approximately 15 cm. Part (c) requires suggesting two practical difficulties causing inaccuracy. Part (d) provides a triangular illuminated object shape and asks to draw the expected focused image on the screen.

p6-190.text: A student investigates reflection using a plane mirror, a ray-trace sheet, and optical pins. On a ray-trace sheet showing a mirror line MR, the student draws a normal NL passing through its centre A and an incident ray AB at an angle of incidence of 30 degrees. Pins P1 and P2 are placed along AB. Viewing the images from a specific direction, the student aligns pins P3 and P4 so they appear directly behind the images of P1 and P2. The student joins P3 and P4, extends the line to meet NL, and measures the angle of reflection r. The procedure is repeated with the sheet turned 180 degrees. Finally, the student suggests a practical reason why the lines may not meet exactly at point A and states experimental precautions.

p6-191.text: A student investigates the refraction of light through a transparent block using a ray-trace sheet, a rectangular block ABCD, and optical pins. A normal NL is drawn through point N on the lower boundary DC, crossing upper boundary AB at E. Pin P1 is placed at N and viewed through side AB, with pins P2 and P3 aligned with its image. The connecting line of P2 and P3 is extended to cross NL at F. The lengths of EN and EF are measured to calculate the refractive index n using n = a / b. Precautions for ensuring reliable results are considered, and a second method involving the block standing on edge is evaluated for reliability.

p6-192.text: Students investigate reflection using a plane mirror on a ray-trace sheet. First, they draw a normal and an incident ray at an angle of 30 degrees to the normal. Using pin positions P3 and P4, students measure the reflected angle alpha for different mirror rotation angles theta. They record their readings in a table, plot a graph of alpha against theta, find the gradient of the line, complete a derived table for (alpha - alpha0), and suggest the relationship between these angular changes. Finally, they state an experimental precaution to improve accuracy.

p6-193.text: A student determines the focal length of a converging lens using an illuminated object, lens, and screen. Keeping the object-screen distance D fixed at 80.0 cm, the student finds two lens positions where a sharply focused image is formed on the screen, measuring distances x and y from the object to the lens. Questions include labelling these distances on a diagram, calculating d, d^2, and the focal length f using given formulas. Students state two experimental precautions for reliability, describe two differences and one similarity between the two formed images, and suggest a variable to change to check accuracy.

p6-194.text: An IGCSE student investigates shadows by placing an object at various distances d from a lamp, measuring the width w and height h of the shadow on a screen. The student measures the shadow dimensions from a full-size diagram for a given distance, calculates the average side length s using s = (w + h) / 2, and records the values in a table. A graph of s against d is plotted. Questions ask to measure shadow dimensions, complete the table, explain the usefulness of calculating s, explain the choice of data intervals, and suggest a reason for limiting the minimum distance between lamp and object.

p6-195.text: An IGCSE class investigates the reflection of light by a plane mirror using a ray-trace sheet. Students are asked to draw a normal to the centre of a mirror, construct an incident ray at 30° to the normal, position a ray box correctly to produce this incident ray, and draw the corresponding reflected ray. Finally, students state two experimental precautions to obtain reliable results, such as viewing pins/rays carefully or keeping the ray thin and sharp.

p6-196.text: A class determines the magnification of an image produced by a lens using an illuminated object, a converging lens, and a screen on a bench. Students measure the object distance u and image distance v from diagram measurements. Using the scale given, actual distances U and V are calculated. The student measures the image height h and object height x, calculating the magnification ratio h/x and comparing it with v/u. Additional questions ask to state a statement and justification regarding whether the results support the suggested relationship, list precautions for reliable results, identify differences between image and object, and suggest a focusing precaution.

p6-197.text: An IGCSE class investigates refraction of light through a transparent block using a ray-trace sheet. On Fig. 4.1, students label points on the incident ray and draw a refracted ray at a specified angle of refraction into the block to meet side CD, predicting and drawing the emergent ray H. Pins P3 and P4 are marked at suitable positions for viewing the images of P1 and P2 through the block. Two precautions for reliable results are stated. Finally, the experiment is repeated with the block turned through 90 degrees, and students state whether the resulting angle of refraction supports the suggestion that it should remain the same.

p6-198.text: Students investigate the magnification produced by a converging lens using an illuminated object, lens, and screen. First, students measure the height h_0 of the triangular object in a diagram. For various object-lens distances u, the image height h_i is measured and recorded in a table. Students calculate S = h_0 / h_i for each row. A graph of S against u is plotted, the gradient G of the graph is determined, and the focal length f of the lens is calculated using f = 1 / G.

p6-199.text: Students investigate the position of the image in a plane mirror using a ray-trace sheet, pins, and a mirror represented by line MR. Pins P_1 and P_2 mark an incident ray, while pins P_3 and P_4 locate the reflected ray. Students draw lines connecting these pins and extend them beyond the mirror. The procedure is repeated with a different angle of incidence using marked positions C and D, and the intersection point Y of the extended lines is labeled. Students measure the perpendicular distances a from P_1 to the mirror and b from Y to the mirror, state whether their results support the suggestion that a equals b with justification, and suggest a precaution for placing pins.

p6-200.text: Students determine the focal length of a lens using an illuminated object, a converging lens, and a screen. The object distance u and image height h are recorded in a table with calculated values of 1/h. Part (a) requires plotting a graph of u against 1/h. Part (b) asks to determine the gradient G of the graph with clear indications shown. Part (c) involves calculating the focal length f using f = G / 1.5 to a suitable number of significant figures. Finally, part (d) asks to state two experimental precautions to obtain reliable results.

p6-201.text: Students investigate the magnification produced by a converging lens using an illuminated triangle, a lens, and a screen. Part (a) requires measuring u and the total distance d from Fig. 5.1, then calculating magnification m using m = (d - u) / u. Part (b) asks to measure the object height h_o from Fig. 5.2 and image height h_i from Fig. 5.3, then calculate another magnification value M = h_i / h_o. Part (c) asks whether findings support the theory that m and M should be the same, with justification. Part (d) asks for a difficulty and solution when measuring image height, and a further precaution for reliability.

p6-202.text: Students determine the focal length of a converging lens using an illuminated object, lens, and screen. They measure distances u and v from the diagram, calculate product uv and sum (u+v), and compute x = uv / (u+v). Using the scale of the diagram, they calculate the focal length f. A student suggests a value for v and considers the range of values for a well-focused image. Finally, students state two precautions to obtain reliable results in the lens experiment.

p6-203.text: Students determine the focal length of a converging lens. They measure object distance u and image distance v in mm from a diagram, calculate uv and (u+v), and find the first focal length f1. Then, using new values of u and v obtained by moving the lens, they calculate a second focal length f2. They state whether the results support the suggestion that f1 equals f2 with justification, list two precautions for reliable results, and sketch the inverted image formed on the screen by a triangular object.

p6-204.text: An IGCSE class investigates the reflection of light by a plane mirror on a ray-trace sheet. Students draw a normal, place pins, position a mirror on lines CD and EF, and measure angles to determine the relationship between angle alpha and angle theta. Part (a) asks to draw a normal and label pin positions. Part (b) asks to draw a line through pins and measure an angle. Part (c) involves repeating the procedure for a second mirror position. Part (d) requires stating whether the results support the suggestion that theta equals 2 alpha and justifying with values. Part (e) asks for two precautions for accurate results.

p6-205.text: An IGCSE class determines the focal length of a lens using an illuminated object, a converging lens, and a screen on a bench. Part (a) asks students to measure lengths d and x from a diagram drawn one-tenth actual size, and calculate the actual distances D and X. Part (b) uses a second lens position to form a diminished image, recording distance Y and calculating the focal length f using the given equation f = XY / D. Part (c) requires comparing two focal length values to test a theory, with justification. Part (d) asks to state a practical precaution to obtain a reliable result in lens experiments.

p6-206.text: A student measures small glass spheres. Part (a) asks for a diagram showing how to arrange a 30 cm rule and two rectangular wooden blocks to measure the diameter of one sphere. Part (b) involves a measuring cylinder containing water: students show the correct line of sight for an accurate reading, record the initial water volume V, and then calculate the volume V_1 of a single sphere after 15 spheres are added to raise the water level to 78 cm^3.

p6-207.text: An IGCSE class determines the refractive index of a transparent block using a ray-trace sheet. Part (a) requires drawing a normal to side AB, marking point N at 4.0 cm from E, drawing line NF at an angle of 20° to the normal, and measuring its length a. Part (b) uses pins P_1 to P_4 to trace the refracted ray through the block, finding points G and H, measuring the length b of line FH, and calculating the refractive index n = b/a. Part (c) asks for a practical precaution to obtain accurate readings.

p6-208.text: Students investigate the refraction of light using a transparent block on a ray-trace sheet. They draw a normal at the centre of side AB, label point E, and construct an incident line at an angle of incidence i = 30°. They mark pin positions P1 and P2, view them through side CD, and place P3 and P4 to trace the emergent ray meeting CD at G. They draw the refracted ray GE, measure the angle of refraction r, and calculate the ratio i/r for two different angles. Finally, they evaluate whether their results support the suggestion that the ratio i/r is a constant.

p6-209.text: Students carry out a refraction experiment using a rectangular glass block and optical pins on a blank sheet. They draw a 10 cm line representing one side of the glass block labeled AB, construct a normal at its centre, and draw an incident line EF at an angle of 30° to the normal. They indicate suitable positions for two optical pins P1 and P2 along the incident line to ensure accurate ray tracing. Finally, they suggest a practical reason why experimental results might differ slightly from theoretical expectations.

p6-210.text: Students determine the focal length of a converging lens using an illuminated object, lens, and screen. They calculate the product uv values and complete the table with units. Students then plot a graph of uv against d, draw a line of best fit, determine the gradient G of the graph showing their working, and state the focal length f of the lens to a suitable number of significant figures.

p6-211.text: An IGCSE class investigates the focal length of a converging lens using an illuminated object, lens, and screen set up on a bench. Students measure object distance u and image distance v from a scaled diagram, convert to actual values, and complete a table calculating 1/u and 1/v. They plot a graph of 1/v against 1/u starting both axes at the origin, find the x-intercept p and y-intercept q, calculate their average z, and determine the focal length f using f = 1/z.

p6-214.text: Students investigate the effect of an electromagnet on an iron block placed on a balance as the current is increased. In part (a), students draw a circuit diagram containing a variable resistor and an ammeter connected to the power supply and electromagnet. In part (b), students calculate values of M by subtracting balance readings m from m0, complete Table 4.1, and state and justify whether M is proportional to I based on the results.

p6-215.text: A student investigates a power supply using a circuit with a resistance wire, ammeter, voltmeter, and a sliding crocodile clip. In part (a), the student reads potential difference V0 and current I0 from meter dials and calculates resistance R0. In part (b), the student calculates 1/I values for different wire lengths l and records them in Table 3.1. In part (c), they plot a graph of l against 1/I. In part (d), they determine the gradient G and calculate the electromotive force E. In part (e), they state and explain which length l is most affected by the ammeter resistance.

p6-216.text: A student investigates the effect of the length of resistance wire on the potential difference across a lamp. The student completes a circuit diagram by adding a voltmeter across the lamp, then takes a reading from a voltmeter dial for length l = 0.200 m. Given other readings in a table, the student predicts how increasing length affects lamp brightness, analyzes whether potential difference is directly proportional to length, suggests reasons for slight differences in repeat readings, and states a safety precaution for working with resistance wires.

p6-217.text: A student determines the resistance of a resistance wire using a circuit with an ammeter, voltmeter, and sliding contact. The student records voltmeter and ammeter readings for length l = 10.0 cm from meter dials, completes table headings, plots a graph of potential difference V against length l, writes a conclusion about the current in the circuit as the sliding contact position changes with justification, and determines a value of V_L from the graph for a given length l = 60.0 cm.

p6-218.text: A student investigates the resistance of a resistance wire using a power supply, ammeter, and crocodile clip. The student draws a voltmeter in the circuit, reads values of potential difference and current from meter dials for a length l = 90.0 cm, and completes a table with given values for other lengths. Calculations involve determining the resistance R and R/l for each length, and predicting the resistance of a 25.0 cm wire. A reason for non-identical results among students is requested, followed by completing a circuit diagram to include a variable resistor to prevent the wire from becoming hot.

p6-219.text: A student determines the resistance of a resistance wire using a circuit containing a power supply, ammeter, voltmeter, and a sliding contact C. The student records the current from an ammeter diagram, records potential difference values across various lengths l of the wire, and calculates V/l ratios in a table. A conclusion is ticked and justified based on these values. The resistance of a 100 cm length of wire is calculated using V and I values, giving an answer to a suitable number of significant figures with units. Ways to minimise temperature rise and the circuit symbol for a variable resistor are also required.

p6-220.text: A student investigates electrical resistance using a circuit with a resistor P and a lamp L. She reads current and voltage from analogue meters, calculates resistances using R = V / I, compares resistance values for different resistors P and Q, suggests a method to confirm temperature changes in a lamp filament, completes a parallel circuit diagram containing two resistors, a lamp, and a voltmeter, and names a component to control the current.

p6-221.text: A student determines the resistance of a resistance wire using a power supply, ammeter, voltmeter, and a sliding contact C. She records current from an ammeter and potential difference values for various lengths l of the resistance wire in a table. She calculates missing resistance values using R = V / I, completes table headings, concludes the relationship between resistance and length, estimates potential difference, calculates resistance for a specific length, and suggests a precaution to minimise temperature rise in the wire.

p6-222.text: A student investigates how the resistance of a filament lamp varies with potential difference using a slide wire. The student draws a voltmeter in parallel with the lamp on a circuit diagram, then reads analogue meters to obtain the potential difference and current for a wire length of 20.0 cm. After calculating resistance using R = V / I and entering it into a table, the student plots a graph of resistance against wire length. From the graph and the observed lamp brightness, the student states and justifies how resistance changes with filament temperature. Finally, the student completes a circuit diagram showing a variable resistor replacing the slide wire.

p6-223.text: A student investigates the electrical power dissipated by different resistors in a d.c. circuit. The student draws a voltmeter symbol connected in parallel across a resistor in a circuit diagram, reads an analogue ammeter and voltmeter, and records the values in a data table with correct units for resistance, current, and potential difference. The student calculates the power supplied to each resistor using P = I × V to a consistent number of significant figures. Finally, the student describes the trend in power as resistance increases and suggests two practical modifications to the procedure to investigate the relationship in greater detail.

p6-224.text: A student determines the resistance of a piece of wire using a circuit with an ammeter, a power supply, a sliding contact, and a voltmeter. The student records the current from an analogue ammeter and the potential difference from an analogue voltmeter for a wire length of 20.0 cm. After completing the table column headings, the student plots a graph of potential difference against length, determines the gradient of the best-fit line, and calculates the resistance per centimetre of the wire, stating the correct unit.

p6-225.text: Students determine the resistance per unit length of a wire X. They complete a circuit diagram by drawing a voltmeter connected across wire X and read the potential difference from an analogue voltmeter scale. They then plot a graph of potential difference against current, find the gradient of the graph, measure a diagram of wire X to calculate its actual length using a scale factor, and calculate the resistance per centimetre to a suitable number of significant figures. Finally, they suggest an improvement to reduce heating in the circuit wire.

p6-226.text: A student investigates the resistance of three wires, A, B, and C. First, the student draws a voltmeter connected across wire A on a circuit diagram, reads potential difference and current from analogue meters, and enters them into a results table. The resistance of each wire is calculated using R = V / I, followed by finding the resistance per unit length r = R / l for each wire. The student evaluates whether r is constant, stating a conclusion with justification. Finally, the student indicates precisely on a diagram where the wire's length should be measured between crocodile clips and suggests a precaution to prevent wire heating.

p6-227.text: Students plan an experiment to investigate whether the resistance of a wire depends on the material from which it is made, using an ammeter, voltmeter, micrometer screw gauge, power supply, variable resistor, and wires of different materials. The plan requires drawing a suitable circuit diagram to determine resistance, explaining the experimental method and measurements to be taken, identifying key variables to keep constant (such as the length and cross-sectional area/diameter of the wires), and drafting a results table with proper column headings and units.

p6-228.text: The experiment investigates the resistance of two resistance wires AB and CD using a sliding contact, an ammeter, and a voltmeter. Students read potential difference V and current I from analogue meters for a length l = 0.200 m of wire AB and calculate the resistance R using R = V / I. They compare this result with R at l = 0.400 m to state a relationship between length and resistance. Next, they compare the resistance of a single wire AB with the combined resistance of wires AB and CD connected in parallel. Finally, students suggest two reasons why different students might obtain different experimental results.

p6-229.text: Students investigate the resistance of a power supply using a resistance wire, crocodile clip, ammeter, and voltmeter. First, students draw a voltmeter connected across terminals P and Q in a circuit diagram. They read an ammeter scale to complete a table of current and potential difference values. They plot a graph of V on the y-axis against I on the x-axis, draw a best-fit line, and determine its gradient M to find the internal resistance R to an appropriate number of significant figures. Finally, they give a practical reason against using very short wire lengths and draw the standard circuit symbol for a variable resistor.

p6-230.text: Students investigate the relationship between potential difference V and current I for a resistor using a slide wire potential divider circuit. Part (a) asks to draw pointer positions on analogue voltmeter and ammeter scales corresponding to given values. Part (b) involves plotting a V against I graph. Part (c) requires determining the gradient G of the line and stating the resistance R with appropriate unit and significant figures. Part (d) asks to evaluate whether V is directly proportional to I based on the graph. Part (e) asks for a practical procedure or apparatus modification to prevent the slide wire from overheating.

p6-231.text: An investigation into how changing the length of resistance wire in a circuit affects the potential difference across a lamp. Part (a) requires completing a circuit diagram by adding a voltmeter in parallel across the lamp. Part (b) asks to read an analogue voltmeter scale and record the reading in a table. Part (c) asks to predict the effect of wire length on lamp brightness using potential difference data. Part (d) requires evaluating whether potential difference is directly proportional to wire length. Parts (e) and (f) ask for practical reasons for slight variations in repeat readings and a safety precaution when using resistance wires.

p6-232.text: A student heats water using an electrical heater. In part (a), the student reads the potential difference V and current I from voltmeter and ammeter scale diagrams. In part (b), the student reads the temperature from a thermometer scale diagram. In part (c), the student draws a line of sight and eye position on a diagram of a measuring cylinder to demonstrate how to correctly measure the volume of water without parallax error.

p6-233.text: A student investigates the resistance of a lamp filament using a circuit with a resistance wire and sliding contact. In part (a), the student calculates the resistance R = V / I for four lengths of wire and completes the missing units in the table column headings. In part (b), the student evaluates whether the filament is broken when the lamp stops glowing by checking if current is still present. In part (c), the student explains why filament resistance is not constant with reference to brightness and temperature change. In part (d), the student identifies a variable resistor as a replacement for the resistance wire and draws the modified circuit diagram.

p6-234.text: The student plans an investigation to determine how the resistance of a wire depends on its length. The available apparatus includes an ammeter, voltmeter, power supply, variable resistor, switch, connecting leads, resistance wires of different lengths, and a metre rule. The task requires drawing a circuit diagram to determine resistance, explaining the procedure, suggesting suitable lengths of wire, stating controlled variables, and drawing a results table with appropriate column headings.

p6-235.text: A student investigates the resistance of a resistor R using a circuit containing resistance wires AB and CD, a voltmeter, an ammeter, and a wandering lead. Part (a) asks to read analogue scale values for potential difference and current and calculate resistance R. Part (b) asks to evaluate whether given resistance values support the statement that resistance remains constant, justifying the conclusion. Part (c) asks to name a circuit component that can control current in place of the resistance wires and draw the updated circuit diagram.

p6-236.text: A student investigates how the resistance of a lamp changes with potential difference using a slide wire circuit. The student reads ammeter values from dial diagrams for five potential difference settings, records them to two significant figures, and calculates the resistance for each setting using R = V/I. The student plots a graph of resistance against potential difference on a grid and interprets its shape to describe the change in resistance. Finally, the student completes a circuit diagram showing how a variable resistor can replace the slide wire to vary potential difference and current.

p6-237.text: Students investigate the link between the brightness of a filament lamp and its resistance by varying the length of a resistance wire connected in series. The student adds a voltmeter to the circuit diagram, selects the most suitable voltmeter range for a 3V power supply, and marks a specific voltmeter reading on the scale. The student calculates resistance values using R = V/I and draws a conclusion linking brightness to resistance based on observational data. Finally, the student proposes an alternative circuit setup to investigate a lamp requiring a higher voltage.

p6-238.text: Students determine the resistance per unit length of a resistance wire. A circuit diagram is provided containing a power supply, switch, ammeter, and a resistance wire mounted on a metre rule. Students draw a voltmeter in parallel across the length l of the wire. They calculate resistance R for five lengths using R = V / I and complete the table. Next, they plot a graph of R against l and determine its gradient G. Finally, they use G to state the resistance per unit length r to an appropriate number of significant figures with units.

p6-239.text: Students determine the resistance of a resistor using a circuit containing a resistor, a wire with a sliding contact, an ammeter, and a voltmeter. Students read values from analogue voltmeter and ammeter dials and record the potential difference for l = 100.0 cm in a data table. They plot a graph of potential difference V against length l, starting both axes at (0, 0). They determine the y-intercept Y from the graph, calculate the ratio Y / I, and use this to state the resistance R of the resistor with appropriate significant figures and units.

p6-240.text: An experiment investigates the resistance of a lamp filament using a circuit containing a sliding contact on a resistance wire. Students record potential difference and current from analogue meter readings to calculate resistance R = V / I. They describe the expected change in lamp brightness as the sliding contact moves along the wire, suggest a practical reason for slight variations in repeated meter readings, and evaluate a V-I graph of a filament lamp to draw a conclusion about how its resistance changes as current increases.

p6-241.text: An experiment investigates the resistance of a fixed resistor using a circuit with a resistance wire and sliding contact acting as a variable resistor. Students read an analogue voltmeter and ammeter to calculate the resistance using R = V / I. They state how moving the sliding contact affects circuit current, draw the standard circuit symbol for a variable resistor, and explain how to find the gradient of a linear V-I graph.

p6-242.text: Students investigate how wire length affects resistance using crocodile clips and meter readings. In part (a), potential difference V and current I are read from analogue meter dials for wire A and recorded in a table. In part (b), column headings for the table units are completed. In part (c), resistances R for wires A, B, and C are calculated using R = V / I, and a student's claim that R_A = R_B + R_C is evaluated and justified. In part (d), a practical technique to minimize heating effects in the wire during testing is suggested.

p6-243.text: Students investigate the relationship between resistance and length for a resistance wire. In part (a), resistance values R for five different lengths l of wire AB are calculated using R = V / I and recorded in a table. In part (b), a graph of R on the y-axis against l on the x-axis is plotted starting from the origin (0,0). In part (c), students evaluate whether R is directly proportional to l by reference to their graph line. In part (d), a procedure to further extend and test this hypothesis using larger lengths of the same apparatus is suggested.

p6-244.text: Students investigate how the resistance of a wire varies with its length using a circuit with a power supply, ammeter, voltmeter, switch, and resistance wire on a metre rule. Part (a) asks students to calculate resistance R = V / I for six given wire lengths and complete table headers with units. Part (b) requires plotting a graph of R against length l. Part (c) involves determining the gradient G of the line. Part (d) asks to predict the resistance R1 for a 1.00 m length of the wire to an appropriate number of significant figures.

p6-245.text: Students investigate the current in copper wires using laboratory apparatus. Part (a) asks to select the most suitable device from a given list to measure approximately 20 m of copper wire. Part (b)(i) requires drawing a complete circuit diagram to measure current across a wire sample for a range of potential differences. Part (b)(ii) asks how to check if a lamp filament in the circuit is broken without removing the lamp. Part (b)(iii) requires evaluating whether a 0–300 V voltmeter is suitable for measuring p.d. in the circuit and justifying the choice.

p6-246.text: Students investigate the resistance of a wire of varying length x using a power supply, ammeter, voltmeter, and sliding contact. In part (a), they calculate resistance values R using R = V / I for different lengths and complete the table with these values and appropriate column headings. In part (b), they plot a graph of potential difference V against resistance R. In part (c), they determine the gradient G of the plotted line, showing their construction on the graph.

p6-247.text: Students investigate how resistance depends on wire length. In part (a), they read current I from an ammeter scale and potential difference V from a voltmeter scale, calculate the resistance R using R = V / I for a length x = 0.200 m, and complete the table. In part (b), they plot a graph of resistance R against length x. In part (c), they use the graph to find the length l corresponding to a resistance of 1.20 Ω. In part (d), they predict the resistance Z for a 1.50 m length of wire.

p6-248.text: Students investigate potential difference V and current I in a circuit containing a resistance wire with a crocodile clip connected at different positions. Students draw a voltmeter symbol between terminals X and Y on the circuit diagram. They plot a graph of potential difference against current, determine its gradient M, and deduce the internal resistance R of the power supply to an appropriate number of significant figures.

p6-249.text: Students determine the resistance of a fixed resistor R in a circuit with a resistance wire and sliding contact. They complete the missing column heading in a data table showing distance d, potential difference V, and current I. They plot a graph of V against I, calculate the gradient G of the line, and state the value of resistance R to an appropriate number of significant figures.

p6-250.text: An investigation of resistor combinations in circuits. Students measure the potential difference V1 and current I1 from analogue meter scales for two resistors connected in parallel. They calculate the total parallel resistance R_P and 4R_P. Next, they calculate the total resistance R_S for the same resistors connected in series using given values of V2 and I2, and evaluate whether the theoretical relationship R_S = 4R_P holds. Students then draw a circuit diagram with two lamps in series, and explain the function and purpose of adding a variable resistor to the circuit.

p6-251.text: An experiment to investigate how the resistance of a lamp changes with potential difference and brightness. Students add a voltmeter symbol across a lamp in a given circuit diagram. They complete the column headings with units in a data table showing potential difference V, current I, resistance R, and visual observations of lamp brightness. Using R = V / I, they calculate resistance values for different voltages. Finally, students evaluate a claim that the resistance of a lamp remains constant regardless of temperature, justifying their conclusion using calculated resistances and observations of brightness.

p6-252.text: A student investigates the resistance of filament lamps in a circuit. First, a single lamp L1 is connected, and the student reads the potential difference V1 from a voltmeter scale and the current I1 from an ammeter scale to calculate the resistance R1. Next, lamps L2 and L3 are added in series one by one, and their potential differences and currents are recorded to calculate resistances R2 and R3. The student calculates the total resistance R1 + R2 + R3, compares it with 3 × R1, and selects the matching suggestion with justification. Finally, a complete circuit diagram showing all three lamps connected in series is drawn.

p6-253.text: Students investigate combinations of resistors. First, they complete a circuit diagram by adding an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across terminals P and Q. They read potential difference V1 and current I1 from meter dials and calculate single-resistor resistance R1. They repeat measurements for two resistors in series and two resistors in parallel to calculate effective single-resistor resistances R2 and R3 using given formulas. They evaluate whether R1, R2, and R3 are equal based on experimental data. Lastly, they draw the circuit symbol for a potential divider and explain how using it improves the reliability of the resistance determination.

p6-254.text: Students investigate a circuit containing three resistors in series and parallel combinations. Part (a) asks to draw a voltmeter connected across resistor X on a given circuit diagram. Part (b) involves reading an ammeter and voltmeter to record initial current and voltage values in a table, and completing column headings. Part (c) requires evaluating whether current remains constant across different resistor combinations using table data. Part (d) asks to calculate total resistances using R = V / I and determine individual resistances R_Y and R_Z. Part (e) requires drawing a circuit diagram with three resistors in parallel and comparing parallel resistance R_P to series resistance R_S.

p6-255.text: A student investigates the resistance of lamps connected in series and parallel. In part (a), readings from a voltmeter and an ammeter are taken to record potential difference V1 and current I1, then resistance R1 is calculated using R1 = V1 / I1. In part (b), combined resistance R2 of two series lamps is calculated. In part (c), the student evaluates whether the total resistance of three lamps in series equals three times R1, justifying the answer with data. In part (d), a circuit diagram is completed to show three lamps in parallel, a voltmeter measuring potential difference across them, and a variable resistor controlling circuit current.

p6-256.text: A student investigates a circuit containing two lamps in series. First, the student completes a circuit diagram by adding a voltmeter across one lamp. Readings from an ammeter and voltmeters measuring potential differences across individual lamps and both lamps combined are recorded. The student evaluates whether the total potential difference equals the sum of individual potential differences. The resistance of one lamp in series is calculated using R = V / I. Next, a circuit diagram is drawn for the lamps connected in parallel with an ammeter in one branch. Finally, the student explains how temperature affects lamp resistance by comparing resistance values obtained when the lamp is dim versus bright.

p6-257.text: A student investigates the resistance of three resistors connected in series. The potential difference across the first resistor and the total current are read from meter displays, and the resistance R1 is calculated using R = V / I. The student then evaluates whether the three resistors have the same resistance based on experimental values. The combined series resistance is calculated to an appropriate number of significant figures, and the expected total potential difference is identified. Finally, the student completes a circuit diagram showing the three resistors connected in parallel with a voltmeter across them and a variable resistor controlling the overall current.

p6-258.text: A student investigates the electrical power of two lamps connected in series. The student reads potential difference and current from meter scales, then calculates total power P_T and individual powers P_X and P_Y using P = VI. The student evaluates whether the individual powers are equal within the limits of experimental accuracy. In a follow-up test with two different lamps where one is dimly lit and the other does not light, the student assesses whether a filament is broken. Finally, the student draws a circuit diagram showing two lamps connected in parallel with a variable resistor, an ammeter, and a voltmeter.

p6-259.text: A student investigates the resistance of resistors connected in series and parallel. The student reads voltmeter and ammeter scales to determine potential difference V_1 and current I_1 for a single resistor, and calculates its resistance using R = V / I. Combined resistances for two and three resistors in series are calculated similarly. The student draws a needle on an ammeter scale, decides whether R_3 = 3 R_1, and explains how to test if all three resistors have equal resistance. Finally, the student completes a circuit diagram for three resistors in parallel controlled by a variable resistor and explains the role of the variable resistor.

p6-260.text: A student investigates a series and parallel resistor circuit. First, a voltmeter is added to a circuit diagram to measure potential difference across a resistor. The student reads current from an ammeter scale and potential differences across individual resistors and their series combination from voltmeter dials. The student evaluates whether the total potential difference equals the sum of individual potential differences. The combined series resistance is calculated using R = V / I. Next, the student draws a circuit diagram showing two resistors in parallel with an ammeter measuring total current and a voltmeter across the pair, and uses parallel circuit data to verify correct setup.

p6-261.text: An investigation of a circuit containing two lamps in series. The student adds a voltmeter symbol across one lamp in a circuit diagram and reads the current from an analogue ammeter dial. Potential differences across both lamps are read from voltmeter dials and recorded in a table alongside brightness observations. The student explains why a non-glowing lamp does not have a broken filament and relates observed brightness to potential difference values. Total resistance is calculated using R = (V_P + V_Q) / I. Finally, the total series potential difference is compared with the power supply voltage to draw a conclusion.
